title: The next tier of what is asked for — 8 machine-checked theorems of the ℤ/9 vortex deposit and how they are bound
description:
The next tier of what is asked for — 8 machine-checked theorems of the ℤ/9 vortex deposit, one Lean namespace, wing the floor. 8 close by exhaustion over a finite domain (by decide). Every one is sealed live in the append-only ledger.

How these theorems are bound. "Entangled" is used in this deposit's honest sense: correlation by derivation, not quantum entanglement, and no information travels through it.

1 · Shared definitions. 2 definition(s) are used by two or more theorems, binding 2 pair(s); the theorems fall into 7 strand(s), the largest of 2. Most binding: sumPow (2), tri (2). 1 theorem(s) name no definition of the file and stand on their own statement.

2 · Imports. Built on: families.lean. Built on it: no other cluster. Checking this cluster needs 2 file(s): src/proof/demand2.lean, src/proof/families.lean.

3 · The joint address. The 8 sealed receipts fold to 3923cc7a-f137-8f83-a0dc-fb8c4bcaba45. Order-invariant: yes — the same root in reverse order. Altering one receipt changes it: yes, computed on this run. A content-address proves integrity, not truth.

4 · The address lattice. Each theorem sits at the seven ray values its page plots from its receipt, taken mod 9: a point of (ℤ/9)⁷. This cluster's centre is (7, 0, 6, 0, 5, 8, 6). Its nearest clusters, ranked by lift — pairs observed among each theorem's seven nearest points, over the pairs expected by chance from the two clusters' sizes: reversal.lean (3 observed, 0.71 expected, lift 4.23), coin.lean (3 observed, 1.06 expected, lift 2.82), light.lean (3 observed, 1.15 expected, lift 2.6). A lift near 1 is what chance gives. Mean distance between two of its theorems: 15.07; from one of its theorems to a theorem of another cluster: 15.56. A receipt is a hash, so nearness on this lattice is a property of the addresses, not of the mathematics; the mathematical binding is (1) and (2). Chance, measured: over 200 reshufflings of which cluster each point belongs to (seeded, so every rebuild gives the same numbers), a best lift at least this high arose in 29.0% of them — consistent with chance.

Prior art. Wilson’s theorem — John Wilson; first proved by Joseph-Louis Lagrange, 1771; the Catalan conjecture on consecutive perfect powers — Eugène Catalan, 1844; proved by Preda Mihăilescu, 2002 Per-theorem prior-art searches — OEIS, zbMATH Open, OpenAlex, Crossref, arXiv — are recorded, with what was searched, where and when, in the living ledger src/proof/novelty.json. No novelty is claimed here.
